'''''Sweet Lavender''''' is a play in three acts by [[Arthur Wing Pinero]], first performed in 1888.  The sentimental and gently humorous story concerns the romance of Lavender Rolt and Clement Hale, and the complications impeding the course of true love.

==Premiere==
The original production opened on 21 March 1888 at [[Terry's Theatre]] in London, starring [[Edward O'Connor Terry|Edward Terry]] as Dick Phenyl, [[Brandon Thomas (playwright)|Brandon Thomas]] as Geoffrey Wedderburn, [[Carlotta Addison]] as Mrs Rolt, and Rose Norreys and Harry Reeves-Smith in the romantic leads.  The play was so popular that it ran for 684 performances – a conspicuously  long run for the time – until 25 January 1890;<ref>Gaye, p. 1538</ref> on its revival less than a year later it ran for a further 737 nights.<ref>Clark, pp. 10–11</ref>

The play was produced over the next few years in Australia, Canada, Germany, India, Italy, Russia, South Africa, the United States, and the West Indies.<ref>Clark, p. 10; and Salaman pp. 8–9</ref> The [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] production opened in November 1888 at the [[Lyceum Theatre (Broadway)|Lyceum Theatre]] with [[William J. Le Moyne|W J LeMoyne]] and  [[Henry Miller (actor)|Henry Miller]]  in the cast.<ref>[https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1888/11/08/100950112.pdf "Life in Chambers"], ''[[The New York Times]]'', 8 November 1888</ref> The Australian premiere,  in 1889, was presented by and starred [[Frank Thornton (Savoyard)|Frank Thornton]]<ref>Salaman, p. 8</ref>

==Original cast==
[[File:Sweet-Lavender-1888.tif|thumb|300px|Theatre programme from the original run, showing two cast changes since the first night]]
*Mr Geoffrey Wedderburn (of Wedderburn, Green and Hoskett, Bankers, Barnchester)  – [[Brandon Thomas (playwright)|Brandon Thomas]]
*Clement Hale (his adopted son, studying for the bar) – Harry Reeves-Smith
*Dr Delaney (a fashionable physician) – Alfred Bishop
*Dick Phenyl (a barrister) – [[Edward O'Connor Terry|Edward Terry]]
*Horace Bream (a young American) – [[Frederick Kerr]]
*Mr Mew (a solicitor) – Sant Matthews
*Mr Bodger (hairdresser and wig maker) – T C Valentine (later in the run, Prince Miller)
*Mrs Gilfillian (a widow – Mr Wedderburn's sister) – Miss M A Victor
*Minnie (her daughter) – [[Maude Millett]]
*Ruth Rolt (housekeeper and laundress at Brain Court, Temple) – [[Carlotta Addison]]
*Lavender (her daughter) – Rose Norreys (later in the run, Blanche Horlock)

==Synopsis==
The play is set in the Chambers of Mr Phenyl and Mr Hale, No 3, Brain Court, Temple. Springtime. The present day.<ref>From the 1922 revival onwards the play was given as a costume piece, set in 1888.</ref>
*Act 1 – Morning – "Nobody's business"
*Act 2 – Evening of the next day – "Somebody's business"
*Act 3 – A Week afterwards – "Everybody's business"

Ruth Rolt, a housekeeper, has a daughter, Lavender, who is in love with Clement Hale,  who is studying for the bar under a disreputable but lovable barrister, Dick Phenyl.  Clement is the adopted son of Geoffrey Wedderburn, a banker, who wants him to marry his niece, Minnie.  Minnie has another suitor, Horace, an American.  Mrs. Rolt discovers that Wedderburn is not only Clement's adoptive father but also Lavender's real father.  She is very angry and breaks off the relationship between Clement and Lavender.

Wedderburn's bank is threatened with failure; he takes ill and learns humility.  Mrs. Rolt forgives and nurses him, while Lavender flies back into Clement's arms to console him after the financial ruin.  Phenyl unexpectedly offers his own fortune to save the bank and Wedderburn's reputation, and all ends happily.

==Revivals and adaptations==
The play was revived at Terry's in September 1890, and in February 1899.<ref name=g1493>Gaye, p. 1493</ref> It was revived at the [[Ambassadors Theatre (London)|Ambassadors]] in December 1922, and at the [[Lyric, Hammersmith]] in June 1932.<ref name=g1493/> On Broadway the play was revived in 1905 (with Terry in his original role), and again in 1923.<ref>[https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1905/01/08/119114078.pdf "Edward Terry Seen In 'Sweet Lavender'"], ''The New York Times'', 8 January 1905; and [https://www.nytimes.com/1923/12/27/archives/sweet-lavender-arrives-english-company-is-to-open-in-pineros-comedy.html "'Sweet Lavender' Arrives"], ''The New York Times'', 27 December 1923</ref>
